rv.q: That question pervades the 1992 film Death Becomes Her (written by Martin Donovan and David Koepp, and directed by Robert Zemeckis), which has just been turned into the funniest new musical comedy on Broadway.
Everything in the musical is fantastically bigger and bolder
Like its duelling antiheroines, Death Becomes Her refuses to die.
Together they make musical-comedy magic—and musical comedy, when performed this well, never gets old.

The narrative bones of the Zemeckis film, which starred Meryl Streep and Goldie Hawn as homicidal frenemies, remain intact. The self-obsessed actress Madeline Ashton (Megan Hilty, escaping Streep’s ice-queen shadow by running hot) greets her old chum and rival, the drab wannabe writer Helen Sharp (Jennifer Simard), backstage after a Broadway show.
Whatever criticism gets hurled its way, nobody could reasonably say that “Death Becomes Her” looks cheap or lacks entertainment value.

At the end of the 1992 film “Death Becomes Her,” the undead frenemies played by Meryl Streep and Goldie Hawn receive punishment for their vanity. Ghoulish mannequins with puttylike skin, they tumble down church steps and shatter into an unholy rubble of limbs — their comeuppance for downing a potion promising eternal youth and beauty.
Even if the musical doesn’t have a discernible heartbeat, Hilty and Simard ensure “Death Becomes Her” stays fun and fabulous.

The musical adaptation of the 1992 dark comedy starring Meryl Streep and Goldie Hawn has been transformed into a glitzy, effects-heavy spectacle that prioritizes visual dazzle over narrative coherence.
“Death Becomes Her” may be one of the funnier new musicals to splash down on Broadway, in a nearly blinding glare of sequins, in recent seasons.

In The Hills of California, Laura Donnelly’s stage mother trades favors with small-time music-industry men for her daughters’ advancement, and then Donnelly steps in to play that same daughter decades later. Even in Oh, Mary!, the quest for fame in the “legitimate theater” winds its way through violence and vomit.
The relentless, deliciously played, perfectly directed hilarity of Death Becomes Her distinguishes this skillfully executed riot of a Broadway musical.

A virtually perfect big-budget, broad-appeal musical comedy that improves in every way over the 1992 film, director-choreographer Christopher Gattelli’s wildly entertaining vehicle for two of our best singer-actor-comedians on any stage today renders the movie-as-source snipe worthless.
It's high camp and Broadway heaven, need I say more?
Thumbs up, three cheers, and a long, long, long life to Death Becomes Her.
Decadent and a lot of fun, Death Becomes Her is a musical that knows what it is and what its audience wants.
The show is so entertaining you'll find yourself not minding very much.
Directing the new musical, Christopher Gattelli gleefully embraces the material’s inherent tackiness.

The fact that the new Broadway show did away with the movie's super campy opener of Meryl Streep's "Me" the film's only musical number, incidentally and replaced it with the even campier "For the Gaze" tells you everything you need to know about the new production and its mission to go bigger and bawdier at every turn.
It’s Tazewell’s costumes that seemed most fully to express the tone of the show: over-the-top but simultaneously making fun of how over-the-top it is — and having fun doing so.
What “Death Becomes Her” lacks is even a remotely decent score.

Where Death Becomes Her never goes wrong is where Broadway musicals rarely falter: the design departments. It’s these contributions that so frequently allow mediocre works to look like the millions of dollars the producers put up and hope to get back. Here, it’s Tazewell buoying the vehicle along with set designer
Look out world, Death Becomes Her: The Musical may just be the biggest body horror bitch-off on Broadway.
Death Becomes Her might be the best dark musical comedy to come along in decades.

(You really, truly want to revive "Mame"? Here are your stars!) Hilty perfectly delivers the narcissism and insecurity of Madeline Ashton, a mega-star of stage and screen (and two-time Oscar nominee as she reminds everyone at the drop of a hat), whom we first meet at the height of her fame.
Death Becomes Her is a crowd-pleasing hit that deserves to be around forever — well, at least for a good long time.
The number, part of a Broadway show titled “Me Me Me,” is a showstopping kickoff to one of the funniest shows to hit the stage in years.
Watching Hilty and Simard spar, singing the enjoyably apt score and chewing the scenery and each other is the musical event of the season so far.
This show will probably sell out, so get your tickets before the whole thing gets old.
Death Becomes Her is intentional, which allows me to buy into the over the top comedy and violence and lack of limits.
Death Becomes Her is nothing more and nothing less than the perfect guilty pleasure musical.
